title: Galois groups of Keller fibers
plain: Gallagher (2026) built, for every n>=3, a polynomial map C^3->C^3 with constant nonzero Jacobian whose general fibre has exactly n points. Determine the symmetry (monodromy/Galois) group of how those n points are permuted.
math: Let $H_n:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ be Gallagher's Keller map of geometric degree $n$ (A. Gallagher, \emph{An infinite family of counterexamples to the Jacobian Conjecture in dimension three}, Zenodo 2026, doi:10.5281/zenodo.21479195), so $[\mathbb C(x,y,z):H_n^*\mathbb C(X,Y,Z)]=n$. For each $n\ge3$ determine the Galois group of the Galois closure of $\mathbb C(x,y,z)/H_n^*\mathbb C(X,Y,Z)$ (equivalently the monodromy group of the $n$-sheeted covering over a general point), as a permutation group of degree $n$; and the arithmetic group over $\mathbb Q$.
review_note: O

title: Keller maps injective on integer points
plain: Take a polynomial map of 3-space with integer coefficients whose Jacobian determinant is identically 1 (a Keller map). Show that if it never sends two different integer points to the same point, then it is a polynomial automorphism.
math: Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y,z]^3$ with $\det JF\equiv 1$. Prove that if $F|_{\mathbb{Z}^3}$ is injective, then $F$ has a polynomial inverse (equivalently, by Bia{\l}ynicki-Birula--Rosenlicht, $F$ is injective on $\mathbb{C}^3$).
review_note: T

title: Keller monodromy is everything
plain: Since 2026 there are polynomial maps of 3-space with constant nonzero Jacobian that are not invertible (counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture), and every number n >= 3 of points in a generic fibre occurs. Show that for every n the fibre points can be permuted in every possible way by going around loops, i.e. the monodromy group can be the full symmetric group S_n.
math: Prove that for every $n\ge3$ there is a polynomial map $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with $\det JF\in\mathbb C^{\times}$, of geometric degree $[\mathbb C(x):\mathbb C(F)]=n$, whose geometric monodromy group (the Galois group of the Galois closure of $\mathbb C(x_1,x_2,x_3)/\mathbb C(F_1,F_2,F_3)$, acting on the $n$ generic fibre points) is $S_n$.
review_note: O

title: Closed-form Euler blow-up
plain: Smooth compactly supported starting data for the 3D Euler equations that blow up in finite time are now known to exist, but the construction is an infinite iterative series. Give such data as an explicit formula.
math: Find an explicit divergence-free $u_0=\nabla\times\big(P(x)e^{-|x|^2}\big)$ with $P\in\mathbb{Q}[x_1,x_2,x_3]^3$ (or another explicitly specified finite closed-form class) such that the unforced 3D incompressible Euler solution on $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $u(0)=u_0$ has finite maximal smooth lifespan.
review_note: T

title: Drum tones of superellipses
plain: Take the region |x|^p + |y|^p <= r^p, scaled to have area 1. At p = 2 it is a disk, which has the lowest possible bass note of any region of that area (Faber–Krahn). As p grows to infinity it becomes a square, whose note is higher. Show that the note rises steadily the whole way from p = 2 to infinity.
math: For $p\in[2,\infty)$ let $D_p=\{(x,y):|x|^p+|y|^p\le r_p^p\}$ with $r_p$ chosen so that $|D_p|=1$, and let $\lambda_1(p)$ be the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of $-\Delta$ on $D_p$. Prove that $\lambda_1$ is strictly increasing on $[2,\infty)$, with $\lambda_1(2)=\pi j_{0,1}^2$ and $\lambda_1(p)\uparrow2\pi^2$ as $p\to\infty$.
review_note: I

title: Multiplicities on the Fermat quartic
plain: The surface x^4+y^4+z^4 = 1 has exactly the 48 symmetries of a cube. Show its Laplace eigenvalues repeat no more often than those symmetries force (at most 3 times), except possibly for finitely many eigenvalues.
math: Let $S=\{x^4+y^4+z^4=1\}\subset\mathbb R^3$ with the induced metric (isometry group the hyperoctahedral group of order 48, whose irreducible representations have dimension $\le3$). Prove that all but finitely many eigenvalues of $\Delta_S$ have multiplicity $\le3$.
review_note: F

title: Frozen vortices for Kuramoto on a cube
plain: Identical Kuramoto oscillators sit on the grid of a cube's surface. Besides full synchrony, there is a 'longitude' state with a vortex at the centre of the top face and an antivortex at the centre of the bottom face. Prove that this state is a linearly stable equilibrium for every grid size.
math: Let $Q_n$ be the vertex–edge graph of the $n\times n$ subdivided surface of the cube, and $\dot\theta_i=\sum_{j\sim i}\sin(\theta_j-\theta_i)$. Prove that for every odd $n\ge3$ there is an equilibrium $\theta^*$ with the cube's 4-fold rotational symmetry about the vertical axis and winding number $\pm1$ around the central plaquettes of the top and bottom faces, whose Jacobian (the Laplacian with edge weights $\cos(\theta^*_j-\theta^*_i)$) has kernel exactly $\mathrm{span}(\mathbf 1)$ and is otherwise positive. (More generally: for which $n$ does $Q_n$ have a stable non-synchronous equilibrium?)
review_note: T

title: Two vortices on a cube
plain: Two identical point vortices moving on the surface of a cube form a two-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian system with no continuous symmetry, so there is no second conserved quantity to make it integrable. Prove their motion is genuinely chaotic.

otin\{v_i\}$. On $M=\{(z_1,z_2):z_1

otin\{v_i\}\}$ with $\omega=dA(z_1)+dA(z_2)$, let $H=G(z_1,z_2)+	frac12(R(z_1)+R(z_2))$. Prove that the Hamiltonian flow has a compact invariant set, inside one energy level, on which its topological entropy is positive.
review_note: T

title: Non-flat free-boundary minimal disks in the superball
plain: In a round ball the only free-boundary minimal disks are flat slices through the centre (Nitsche). The superball x^4+y^4+z^4 <= 1 has nine flat ones, cut by its mirror planes. Is there also one that is not flat? A natural candidate has threefold symmetry about the diagonal (1,1,1).
math: For $p>2$ let $B_p=\{|x|^p+|y|^p+|z|^p\le1\}$. Decide whether $B_4$ (more generally $B_p$) contains an embedded minimal disk $\Sigma$ with $\partial\Sigma\subset\partial B_p$, meeting $\partial B_p$ orthogonally, that is not contained in a plane. Specifically, show that there is one invariant under the rotation by $2\pi/3$ about the axis $\mathbb R(1,1,1)$ and under $v\mapsto-v$.
review_note: W

title: Rotation-proof lattice-point-poor shapes
plain: Among convex shapes of area A, how few lattice points can a shape be guaranteed to contain under every rotation about the origin? Can any shape do much better than a disc centred at the origin?
math: For $A>0$ let $m(A)=\inf\{\sup_{\theta}\#(\rho_\theta K\cap\mathbb Z^2): K\subset\mathbb R^2\text{ compact convex},\ |K|=A\}$. Decide whether $m(A)\ge A-O_\varepsilon(A^{1/4+\varepsilon})$.
review_note: T

title: Rupert superballs
plain: A cube can pass through a hole drilled in a copy of itself; a round ball cannot. Show that every superball between them, |x|^p+|y|^p+|z|^p ≤ 1 with p > 2, can.
math: Let $B_p=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x_1|^p+|x_2|^p+|x_3|^p\le1\}$ and $q=p/(p-1)$. Prove that for every $p\in(2,\infty)$ there are orthogonal projections $\pi_1,\pi_2$ of $\mathbb R^3$ onto planes and a rigid motion $\rho$ with $\rho(\pi_1(B_p))\subset\operatorname{int}\pi_2(B_p)$. By central symmetry this is equivalent to: there are orthonormal pairs $(a_1,a_2),(b_1,b_2)$ in $\mathbb R^3$ with $\|\cos t\,b_1+\sin t\,b_2\|_q>\|\cos t\,a_1+\sin t\,a_2\|_q$ for all $t$.
review_note: N

title: Prime Markov triples
plain: Markov triples are positive integer solutions of x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz. Are there infinitely many in which all three numbers are prime?
math: Decide whether infinitely many solutions $(x,y,z)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^3$ of $x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz$ have $x,y,z$ all prime.
review_note: W

title: Burgers with degenerate critical dissipation
plain: Critical half-Laplacian dissipation keeps Burgers smooth. Let that dissipation switch off quadratically at one point of the circle. Do shocks form there?
math: Let $a(x)=1-\cos x$ and consider $u_t+uu_x+\Lambda^{1/2}\big(a\,\Lambda^{1/2}u\big)=0$ on $\mathbb{T}$, $\Lambda=(-\partial_x^2)^{1/2}$. Decide whether every real $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb{T})$ yields a global smooth solution.
review_note: L

title: Minimal-mass blow-up with reflection
plain: Consider the 2D Schrödinger equation in which the self-interaction at each point uses the density at the mirror point -x. Below the ground-state mass, solutions exist forever. Show that the only solutions that blow up with exactly the ground-state mass are the explicit pseudo-conformal ground-state solutions centred at the origin.
math: Let $Q>0$ be the radial solution of $\Delta Q-Q+Q^3=0$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Consider $iu_t+\Delta u+|u(-x,t)|^2u=0$ with $u_0\in H^1(\mathbb R^2)$ and $\|u_0\|_{L^2}=\|Q\|_{L^2}$. Prove that if $u$ blows up at a finite time $T$, then there are $\theta\in\mathbb R$ and $\lambda>0$ with $u(t,x)=e^{i\theta}\frac{\lambda}{T-t}\,Q\!\Big(\frac{\lambda x}{T-t}\Big)\exp\!\Big(i\frac{\lambda^2}{T-t}-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}\Big)$.
review_note: T

title: Riesz-transform Schrodinger equation
plain: Couple a 2D Schrodinger wave to the Riesz transform of its own density. Mass is conserved, but there is no energy. Do smooth solutions live forever?
math: Consider $iu_t+\Delta u=u\,R_1(|u|^2)$ on $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^2$, $\widehat{R_1f}(\xi)=-i\frac{\xi_1}{|\xi|}\hat f(\xi)$. Decide whether every $u_0\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^2)$ gives a global solution in $C(\mathbb{R},H^1)$.
review_note: C

title: Shifted Fujita equation
plain: In the plane, every positive solution of u_t = Delta u + u^2 blows up (u^2 is exactly Fujita-critical in dimension 2). Does this survive when u^2 is replaced by the product of the values of u one unit to the left and one unit to the right?
math: Let $e=(1,0)$. Prove or disprove: for every $0\le u_0\in C_c(\mathbb R^2)$ with $u_0\not\equiv0$, the solution of $u_t=\Delta u+u(x-e,t)\,u(x+e,t)$ on $\mathbb R^2$ blows up in finite time.
review_note: L

title: Unforced blow-up near the forced one
plain: The 2026 forced Navier–Stokes blow-up uses a force that is smooth through the blow-up time. Can the force be made to vanish identically at the blow-up instant while staying smooth up to and including that instant?
math: Do there exist $T>0$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times(0,\infty))$ with $f(\cdot,T)\equiv0$ such that the 3D Navier–Stokes solution on $\mathbb R^3$ with $u_0=0$ and force $f$ satisfies $\limsup_{t\uparrow T}\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty}=\infty$? (Requiring $f\equiv0$ on $[T-\delta,T]$ for some $\delta>0$ instead would be equivalent to unforced blow-up from smooth data, which is the Millennium problem.)
review_note: A

title: Random Wang tiles
plain: (Corrected.) Draw n Wang tiles whose four edge colours are chosen uniformly at random from c colours, and let c grow with n ≈ λc². How likely is the set to tile the plane? Show the probability has a limit F(λ) and find the critical λ above which tiling is almost certain.
math: Let $T_1,\dots,T_n$ be i.i.d. Wang tiles, each with its four edge colours i.i.d. uniform in $[c]$ and no rotations allowed. Let $n=\lfloor\lambda c^2\rfloor$ and $c\to\infty$. Prove that $F(\lambda)=\lim_{c\to\infty}\Pr(\{T_i\}\text{ tiles }\mathbb Z^2)$ exists for every $\lambda>0$. Determine $\lambda_c=\inf\{\lambda:F(\lambda)=1\}$; a first-moment heuristic suggests $\lambda_c=1$. Also determine $F$ on $(0,\lambda_c)$.
review_note: A

title: Period-doubling torus bundles
plain: Build a once-punctured torus bundle by reading the period-doubling word as a product of the two basic shear matrices. Show its hyperbolic volume per letter settles to a limit as the word grows.
math: Let $W_n\in\{a,b\}^{2^n}$ be the length-$2^n$ prefix of the fixed point of $a\mapsto ab,\ b\mapsto aa$ ($n\ge1$). Let $\phi_n\in SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ be the product obtained from $W_n$ via $a\mapsto R=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $b\mapsto L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, and let $M_n$ be the once-punctured torus bundle with monodromy $\phi_n$ (hyperbolic since $W_n$ contains both letters). Prove that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{vol}(M_n)/2^n$ exists.
review_note: L

title: Thue–Morse Lorenz knots
plain: Turn the first 2^n letters of the Thue–Morse word into a periodic orbit of the Lorenz flow, and so into a knot K_n. For n >= 4 these knots appear to be hyperbolic. Their volume grows only in proportion to n, the logarithm of the word length, not in proportion to the length itself. Prove that, and find the constant.
math: Let $K_n$ be the Lorenz knot with Lorenz word $t_0t_1\cdots t_{2^n-1}$ (the length-$2^n$ Thue–Morse prefix, $0\mapsto x$, $1\mapsto y$; this word is primitive, since Thue–Morse is overlap-free and $t_{[0,2^n)}=w\bar w$). Prove that $S^3\setminus K_n$ is hyperbolic for all $n\ge4$ and that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{vol}(S^3\setminus K_n)/n$ exists and is positive. Determine the limit.
review_note: T

title: Is R(3,10) equal to 40 or 41?
credit: Radziszowski dynamic survey 'Small Ramsey Numbers'; Angeltveit (2023/2025).
premise_risks: Angeltveit's upper bound is computer-assisted; if it had an error the range would revert to 40-42
An unpublished construction or nonexistence proof could exist
plain: The Ramsey number R(3,10) is the fewest people at a party that guarantees either 3 mutual acquaintances or 10 mutual strangers. It is known to be 40 or 41, and nobody knows which. Settle it: either build a 40-vertex triangle-free graph with no 10 pairwise non-adjacent vertices, or show none exists.
math: Let $R(3,10)$ be the least $n$ such that every graph on $n$ vertices contains $K_3$ or an independent set of size $10$. Known: $40\le R(3,10)\le 41$. Decide whether there exists a triangle-free graph $G$ on $40$ vertices with $\alpha(G)\le 9$ (equivalently whether $R(3,10)=41$).
review_note: Known: Lower bound 40: Exoo (1989), a (3,10)-graph on 39 vertices. Upper bound 41: V. Angeltveit, 'R(3,10) <= 41', arXiv:2401.00392, Electron. J. Combin. 32(4) (2025) P4.30, improving 42 (Goedgebeur-Radziszowski 2013). Pandey-Ravi, arXiv:2601.03572 (Jan 2026), study structural properties of hypothetical critical graphs, quoting the older range 40-42 and assuming R(3,10)=42; they do not settle the value. No 2025-2026 resolution found.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E021: Is R(3,10) equal to 40 or 41?
The Ramsey number R(3,10) is the fewest people at a party that guarantees either 3 mutual acquaintances or 10 mutual strangers. It is known to be 40 or 41, and nobody knows which. Settle it: either build a 40-vertex triangle-free graph with no 10 pairwise non-adjacent vertices, or show none exists.
Informal statement: Let $R(3,10)$ be the least $n$ such that every graph on $n$ vertices contains $K_3$ or an independent set of size $10$. Known: $40\le R(3,10)\le 41$. Decide whether there exists a triangle-free graph $G$ on $40$ vertices with $\alpha(G)\le 9$ (equivalently whether $R(3,10)=41$).
Formalization notes: Claim says every graph on 40 vertices has a triangle or an independent set of size 10, i.e. R(3,10) <= 40. Given the known 40 <= R(3,10) <= 41: Claim true means R(3,10)=40, and ¬Claim (a triangle-free graph on 40 vertices with independence number <= 9 exists) means R(3,10)=41. Adjacency is irreflexive, so a triangle's vertices are automatically distinct.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE021
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin 40),
    (∃ a b c : Fin 40, G.Adj a b ∧ G.Adj b c ∧ G.Adj a c) ∨
    (∃ s : Finset (Fin 40), s.card = 10 ∧ ∀ x ∈ s, ∀ y ∈ s, x ≠ y → ¬ G.Adj x y)
end OpenProblems.QEDE021

title: Four-colour triangle Ramsey number R(3,3,3,3)
credit: Radziszowski survey; Chung (1973); Fettes-Kramer-Radziszowski (2004); Tatarevic (2026 preprint).
premise_risks: The bound 60 is an unrefereed 2026 preprint resting on unverified SAT runs; the safe published bound is 62
Problem may be stated with whichever upper bound the board accepts
plain: Colour every edge of a complete graph with one of four colours. How many vertices force a single-coloured triangle? The answer is known to lie between 51 and 60 (the 60 coming from a 2026 computer-assisted preprint). Narrow or close this gap.
math: Let $R_4(3)=R(3,3,3,3)$ be the least $n$ such that every 4-edge-colouring of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic triangle. Known: $51\le R_4(3)\le 62$ (refereed), and $\le 60$ in a 2026 computer-assisted preprint. Improve either bound, i.e. exhibit a 4-colouring of $K_{51}$ with no monochromatic triangle, or lower the upper bound (below 60, or confirm 60 rigorously). Ultimately determine $R_4(3)$; it is conjectured to be $51$.
review_note: Known: Lower 51: F. Chung (1973). Upper 62: Fettes-Kramer-Radziszowski, Ars Combin. 72 (2004). Upper 60: M. Tatarevic, arXiv:2610.36648 (2026 preprint). It reduces to 296,081 SAT instances (UNSAT by Kissat and CaDiCaL); the reductions are in Lean/Mathlib, but the SAT exclusions are taken as a premise; extensive AI assistance is disclosed. Boza, arXiv:2603.10851 (2026), improves other multicolour bounds and cites 62 for R_4(3).

end OpenProblems.QEDE022

title: Does the Steiner system S(2,6,51) exist?
credit: Handbook of Combinatorial Designs (Abel-Greig table); Banakh-Hetman-Ravsky (2025).
premise_risks: Exact open list taken from arXiv:2511.05191 as summarised; 51 being open should be double-checked against Abel's latest tables
Exhaustive search may be far harder than v=46 so the problem could be practically intractable
plain: Can you choose 6-element groups from 51 objects so that every pair of objects lies together in exactly one group (that would take 85 groups)? The arithmetic allows it, but no one has built one or proved it impossible. This is the smallest such undecided case for groups of size 6.
math: Decide whether there is a family $\mathcal B$ of $6$-subsets of a $51$-set $V$ such that every $2$-subset of $V$ lies in exactly one member of $\mathcal B$ (a $2$-$(51,6,1)$ design; necessarily $|\mathcal B|=85$ and each point is in $10$ blocks).
review_note: Known: Necessary conditions v ≡ 1, 6 (mod 15). The Handbook of Combinatorial Designs (Abel-Greig) listed 29 undecided v. Banakh-Hetman-Ravsky, arXiv:2511.05191 (2025), construct S(2,6,226) and S(2,6,441), leaving 27 open: 51, 61, 81, 166, 231, 256, 261, 286, 316, 321, 346, 351, 376, 406, 411, 436, 471, 501, 561, 591, 616, 646, 651, 676, 771, 796, 801. S(2,6,46) does not exist (Houghten-Thiel-Janssen-Lam, 2001, exhaustive computation).

title: Ramsey multiplicity constant of K_4
premise_risks: Asymptotic constant; Lean formalization would need the limit definition, and 'improve a bound' is not a yes/no claim
plain: In any red/blue colouring of the edges of a huge complete graph, some fraction of all 4-vertex sets must be single-coloured (all 6 edges the same colour). The minimum possible fraction is known only to lie between about 0.0296 and 0.03015. Pin it down further, or find its exact value.
math: Let $c_4=\lim_{n\to\infty}\min_{G,|V(G)|=n}\big(k_4(G)+k_4(\bar G)\big)/\binom n4$. Known: $0.0296<c_4\le U=4551721\cdot 2^{-24}\cdot 3^{-2}<0.030145$ (Parczyk–Pokutta–Spiegel–Szabó). Formal target: improve the upper bound strictly, i.e. prove $c_4<4551721\cdot 2^{-24}\cdot 3^{-2}$ (more generally improve either bound or determine $c_4$).
review_note: Known: Upper: Thomason (1989) < 1/33; Parczyk-Pokutta-Spiegel-Szabo, arXiv:2206.04036, Found. Comput. Math. (2024): c_4 <= 4551721·2^{-24}·3^{-2} < 0.030145 (blow-ups of a 768-vertex Cayley graph). Lower: Niess (arXiv:1207.4714) 0.0287; Sperfeld; Grzesik-Lee-Lidicky-Volec: c_4 > 0.0296 (cited in PPSS). Erdos's conjecture c_4 = 1/32 was refuted by Thomason.

/-! QED-E024: Ramsey multiplicity constant of K_4
In any red/blue colouring of the edges of a huge complete graph, some fraction of all 4-vertex sets must be single-coloured (all 6 edges the same colour). The minimum possible fraction is known only to lie between about 0.0296 and 0.03015. Pin it down further, or find its exact value.
Informal statement: Let $c_4=\lim_{n\to\infty}\min_{G,|V(G)|=n}\big(k_4(G)+k_4(\bar G)\big)/\binom n4$.
Known: $0.0296<c_4\le U:=4551721\cdot 2^{-24}\cdot 3^{-2}\approx 0.0301449$ (upper bound:
Parczyk–Pokutta–Spiegel–Szabó, Found. Comput. Math. 2024, from blow-ups of a 768-vertex Cayley
graph). Formalized target (strict improvement of the best known UPPER bound): prove $c_4 < U$.
Formalization notes:
* `mono G` counts 4-element vertex sets of `G` that are cliques of `G` or of its complement
  `Gᶜ` (i.e. the monochromatic K₄'s of the red/blue colouring "red = edge of G"). A 4-set cannot
  be both, so this is k₄(G) + k₄(Ḡ).
* `m n` = min over all simple graphs on `Fin n` of `mono G / C(n,4)` (an `iInf` over the finite,
  nonempty type `SimpleGraph (Fin n)`; values lie in [0,1], so the real `iInf` is a genuine
  minimum). For n < 4 the ratio is the junk value 0, which is irrelevant below.
* Standard averaging over (n−1)-vertex subsets shows `m n` is nondecreasing for n ≥ 4, so
  c₄ = lim m n = sup_{n≥4} m n exists and m n ≤ c₄ for all n ≥ 4. Hence
  c₄ < U  ⇔  ∃ c < U, m n ≤ c for all large n. We state the right-hand side, which avoids
  defining the limit with junk values. (A single finite graph can never prove it, as m n ≤ c₄;
  a proof needs a sequence, e.g. a better blow-up construction.)
* The known upper bound is non-strict (it is the exact density of a blow-up family), so
  `Claim` is a genuine strict improvement. Proving `Claim` = c₄ < 4551721/(2²⁴·9). Proving
  `¬Claim` = c₄ = 4551721/(2²⁴·9) exactly (the PPSS construction is optimal), given the known
  bound c₄ ≤ U.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE024
noncomputable section
open scoped Classical

/-- Number of monochromatic 4-sets: 4-cliques of `G` plus 4-cliques of the complement. -/

Take algebraic integers all of whose conjugates are positive real numbers, and look at the average of their conjugates (trace divided by degree). Apart from finitely many exceptions this average cannot be small, and the threshold where infinitely many examples start is a constant lambda. $\{\operatorname{tr}(\alpha)/\deg(\alpha)\}$ over totally positive algebraic integers $\alpha$
(equivalently $\liminf\operatorname{tr}(\alpha)/\deg(\alpha)$ as $\deg\alpha\to\infty$). Known:
$1.80220\le\lambda_{\mathrm{SSS}}\le 1.8216$; the lower bound is stated non-strictly
("λ_SSS ≥ 1.80220", arXiv:2609.29298, unrefereed; previous refereed-track bound 1.80203 by

$\lambda_{\mathrm{SSS}} > 1.80220$.

  polynomials `P ∈ ℤ[X]` that are irreducible (over ℤ, equivalently over ℚ by Gauss's lemma for
  monic polynomials) and all of whose complex roots are real and positive. For such `P` of degree
  d, tr(α)/deg(α) = (sum of the d complex roots)/d; `mean P` computes this from the multiset of
  complex roots of `P` (which has exactly d elements since ℂ is algebraically closed; roots are
  simple by irreducibility/separability). Conjugate α's have the same ratio, so working with
  minimal polynomials loses nothing.

  lie in (0, trace]), so "the ratio is < t for infinitely many α (up to conjugacy)" is the same
  as "for α of arbitrarily large degree". Hence λ_SSS = liminf ratio satisfies
  λ_SSS > L  ⇔  ∃ t > L such that only finitely many admissible `P` have `mean P < t`.

  λ_SSS ≤ 1.80220, which together with the 2026 bound means λ_SSS = 1.80220 exactly (if that
  bound is correct; if it fails, ¬Claim just says λ_SSS ≤ 1.80220).
-/

noncomputable section
open Polynomial

/-- `P` is the minimal polynomial of a totally positive algebraic integer. -/
def IsTotPosMinpoly (P : ℤ[X]) : Prop :=
  P.Monic ∧ Irreducible P ∧
    ∀ z ∈ (P.map (Int.castRingHom ℂ)).roots, z.im = 0 ∧ 0 < z.re

/-- Trace over degree: the average of the (complex) roots of `P`. -/
def mean (P : ℤ[X]) : ℝ :=
  (((P.map (Int.castRingHom ℂ)).roots.map Complex.re).sum) / (P.natDegree : ℝ)

/-- `λ_SSS > 1.80220`. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ t : ℝ, (180220 / 100000 : ℝ) < t ∧
    {P : ℤ[X] | IsTotPosMinpoly P ∧ mean P < t}.Finite

/-! QED-E038: Squeezing the square-lattice site percolation threshold
Colour each square of an infinite chessboard black independently with probability p. There is a critical p above which an infinite connected black cluster appears; simulations put it at about 0.5927, but nobody has a formula. The best proved statements only say it lies between 0.556 and 0.6669. Prove a tighter bound on either side.
Informal statement: Let $p_c=p_c^{\mathrm{site}}(\mathbb Z^2)$ be the critical probability for
Bernoulli site percolation on the square lattice (nearest-neighbour adjacency). Known
rigorously: $0.556 < p_c < 0.666894$ (lower: van den Berg–Ermakov 1996; upper: Wierman–Oberly,
reported to six decimals). Formal target (improvement of the UPPER bound at its published
precision): prove $p_c < 0.6668$.
Formalization notes:
* Configurations: `ω : ℤ × ℤ → Bool`, `ω x = true` meaning site x is open (black). The law
  `perc p` is Mathlib's infinite product measure `Measure.infinitePi` of Bernoulli(p) measures
  (`PMF.bernoulli p h` gives `true` with probability p), i.e. the product Bernoulli measure on
  {0,1}^(ℤ²) with the product σ-algebra.
* Clusters: sites are adjacent iff they differ by 1 in exactly one coordinate (ℓ¹ distance 1).
  The open cluster of the origin is the set of sites reachable from (0,0) along adjacent open
  sites (`Relation.ReflTransGen` of the open-adjacency relation; the step relation requires both
  ends open, so if the origin is closed its "cluster" is {0}). θ(p) = probability that this set
  is infinite (= the origin lies in an infinite open cluster; the event is measurable, being a
  countable union/intersection of cylinder events).
* p_c := sup {p ∈ [0,1] : θ(p) = 0}. θ is nondecreasing in p (standard coupling), so this is the
  usual critical probability; the set contains 0 and is bounded by 1, so `sSup` in `ℝ≥0` is
  meaningful.
* Choice of target: the known bounds are reported as strict inequalities with rounded constants
  (the upper bound is the rounded-up value of an algebraic number), so restating them would not be
  an improvement and their exact values are not encoded here. We take the improvement of the
  upper bound in the fourth decimal: p_c < 0.6668 (any rigorous bound ≤ 0.6668 − ε, e.g. by
  further substitution-method computations). Proving `Claim` = this new upper bound. Proving
  `¬Claim` = p_c ≥ 0.6668 (false according to all numerics, p_c ≈ 0.592746).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE038
noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory
open scoped NNReal ENNReal

/-- Site configurations on `ℤ²`. -/
abbrev Config : Type := ℤ × ℤ → Bool

/-- Nearest-neighbour adjacency on `ℤ²`. -/
def Adj (x y : ℤ × ℤ) : Prop := |x.1 - y.1| + |x.2 - y.2| = 1

/-- One step between adjacent open sites. -/
def OpenStep (ω : Config) (x y : ℤ × ℤ) : Prop := Adj x y ∧ ω x = true ∧ ω y = true

/-- The open cluster of the origin is infinite. -/
def Percolates (ω : Config) : Prop :=
  {z : ℤ × ℤ | Relation.ReflTransGen (OpenStep ω) (0, 0) z}.Infinite

/-- Product Bernoulli(`p`) site percolation measure. -/
def perc (p : ℝ≥0) (h : p ≤ 1) : Measure Config :=
  Measure.infinitePi (fun _ : ℤ × ℤ => (PMF.bernoulli p h).toMeasure)

/-- `θ(p)`: probability that the origin is in an infinite open cluster. -/
def theta (p : ℝ≥0) (h : p ≤ 1) : ℝ≥0∞ := perc p h {ω : Config | Percolates ω}

/-- Critical probability `p_c = sup {p : θ(p) = 0}`. -/
def pc : ℝ≥0 := sSup {p : ℝ≥0 | ∃ h : p ≤ 1, theta p h = 0}

/-- New upper bound `p_c < 0.6668`. -/
def Claim : Prop := (pc : ℝ) < 6668 / 10000

title: Rigorously refute Palásti's parking conjecture in the plane
premise_risks: Weiner (1978) claimed a proof of a Palásti conjecture; the exchange in J. Appl. Prob. indicates it is flawed or about a different model, but I did not read the papers in full
Variants use lattice squares or random sizes; the continuum aligned unit-square version is intended
plain: Drop unit squares (all axis-parallel) one at a time at uniformly random positions in a huge box, keeping each one only if it does not overlap those already placed, until no more fit. Simulations give about 0.5620, so the guess seems wrong, but nobody has proved it. Prove that the planar jamming density is not Rényi's constant squared.
math: Let $\rho_2$ be the jamming limit of random sequential adsorption of aligned unit squares in $[0,L]^2$ as $L\to\infty$; it exists, with $L^1$ and a.s. convergence, by Penrose (2001). Let $c_R=\int_0^\infty\exp\!\left(-2\int_0^t\frac{1-e^{-u}}{u}\,du\right)dt\approx0.747598$ be Rényi's constant. Prove $\rho_2\ne c_R^2$, for instance by proving a rigorous lower bound $\rho_2>c_R^2\approx0.55890$. More generally, give any rigorous non-trivial two-sided bound on $\rho_2$.

Drop unit squares (all axis-parallel) one at a time at uniformly random positions in a huge box, keeping each one only if it does not overlap those already placed, until no more fit. In one dimension the covered fraction tends to Rényi's constant, about 0.7476. Palásti guessed the planar answer is Rényi's constant squared, about 0.5589. Simulations give about 0.5620, so the guess seems wrong, but nobody has proved it. Prove that the planar jamming density is not Rényi's constant squared.
Informal statement: Let $\rho_2$ be the jamming limit of random sequential adsorption of aligned unit squares in $[0,L]^2$ as $L\to\infty$; it exists, with $L^1$ and a.s. convergence, by Penrose (2001). Let $c_R=\int_0^\infty\exp\!\left(-2\int_0^t\frac{1-e^{-u}}{u}\,du\right)dt\approx0.747598$ be Rényi's constant. Prove $\rho_2\ne c_R^2$, for instance by proving a rigorous lower bound $\rho_2>c_R^2\approx0.55890$. More generally, give any rigorous non-trivial two-sided bound on $\rho_2$.
Formalization notes:
* RSA in the box [0,L]² (L ∈ ℕ, L ≥ 2): a unit square is identified with its lower-left corner
  p ∈ [0, L−1]², so it lies inside the box. Arrivals are i.i.d. uniform corners x₁, x₂, … in
  [0, L−1]². The k-th arrival is accepted iff its open square is disjoint from the open squares
  of all previously accepted ones, i.e. iff |p₁ − q₁| ≥ 1 or |p₂ − q₂| ≥ 1 for every accepted q
  (`overlap`). `accepted` runs this rule left to right on a finite list of arrivals.
  (The continuous-time Poisson-arrival version used by Penrose produces the same sequence of
  accepted squares, since only the order of arrivals matters; boundary contacts have
  probability 0 and do not matter.)
* Jamming: the number of accepted squares after k arrivals is nondecreasing in k and bounded by
  L², so it is eventually constant (the jammed state, reached a.s. since any region of positive
  area where a corner could still be accepted is hit eventually); by monotone convergence the
  expected final number is the supremum over k of the expected number after k arrivals. The
  latter is a finite-dimensional Lebesgue integral over ([0,L−1]²)^k divided by its volume
  (L−1)^{2k} (uniform distribution), computed with `lintegral` in `ℝ≥0∞`, so there are no
  integrability side conditions. `rho L` = expected final number / L² = expected covered area
  fraction (each square has area 1).
* Penrose (2001) proves ρ_L → ρ₂ (expectations converge; indeed L¹ and a.s.). Hence
  ρ₂ ≠ c_R² ⇔ ρ_L does not converge to c_R². `Claim` states the latter, which needs no
  separate definition of the limit.

  on (0,∞) (the value at u = 0 is irrelevant, measure zero) and the outer integrand decays like
  t⁻², so both integrals are genuine (no junk 0 from non-integrability).

noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory
open scoped ENNReal Classical

/-- Open unit squares with lower-left corners `p`, `q` overlap. -/
def overlap (p q : ℝ × ℝ) : Prop := |p.1 - q.1| < 1 ∧ |p.2 - q.2| < 1

/-- Accepted corners after processing a list of arrivals in order (RSA rule). -/
def accepted (xs : List (ℝ × ℝ)) : List (ℝ × ℝ) :=
  xs.foldl (fun acc p => if ∀ q ∈ acc, ¬ overlap p q then acc ++ [p] else acc) []

/-- Admissible corners in the box `[0,L]²`. -/
def corners (L : ℕ) : Set (ℝ × ℝ) := Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) ((L : ℝ) - 1) ×ˢ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) ((L : ℝ) - 1)

/-- Expected number of accepted squares after `k` i.i.d. uniform arrivals. -/
def expectedAfter (L k : ℕ) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  (∫⁻ x in Set.pi Set.univ (fun _ : Fin k => corners L),
      ((accepted (List.ofFn x)).length : ℝ≥0∞)) /
    (volume (corners L)) ^ k

/-- Expected jammed covered fraction in the box `[0,L]²`. -/
def rho (L : ℕ) : ℝ := ((⨆ k : ℕ, expectedAfter L k) / ((L : ℝ≥0∞) ^ 2)).toReal

/-- Rényi's parking constant `c_R ≈ 0.747598`. -/
def renyi : ℝ :=
  ∫ t in Set.Ioi (0 : ℝ), Real.exp (-2 * ∫ u in (0 : ℝ)..t, (1 - Real.exp (-u)) / u)

/-- Palásti's conjecture `ρ₂ = c_R²` fails. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ¬ Filter.Tendsto rho Filter.atTop (nhds (renyi ^ 2))

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE046

title: Does the trefoil have a symbiont?
credit: Brittenham & Hermiller, arXiv 2601.18757 (2026), Cor. 4.2 and Sec. 3/5
premise_risks: Fast-moving area: a late-2026 preprint could settle u(10_6)
Mirror conventions: the bound u(3_1#10_6) ≤ 3 is for a specific mirror pairing
u(10_6)=2 would not settle the trefoil question, since another partner could exist
plain: The unknotting number of a knot is the fewest crossing changes needed to turn it into an unknotted loop. In 2025 it was shown that tying two knots together end to end can need fewer changes than the two knots need separately, and in 2026 that every torus knot except possibly the trefoil has a partner like this. Does the trefoil, the simplest knot, also have such a partner? The most likely candidate is the 10-crossing knot 10_6, whose own unknotting number is still unknown (it is 2 or 3).
math: Write $u(K)$ for the unknotting number and $\#$ for connected sum. Knots $K,K'$ are symbionts if $u(K\#K')<u(K)+u(K')$. Is there a knot $K$, with some choice of mirror image, such that $u(3_1\#K)<1+u(K)$? By Scharlemann's theorem any such $K$ has $u(K)\ge2$. Concrete subquestion: is $u(10_6)=3$? Brittenham–Hermiller prove $u(3_1\#10_6)\le3$ for the mirror choice with $|\sigma(3_1\#10_6)|=2$, so $u(10_6)=3$ would give a positive answer.

In 2025 it was shown that tying two knots together end to end can need fewer changes than the two knots need separately, and in 2026 that every torus knot except possibly the trefoil has a partner like this. Does the trefoil, the simplest knot, also have such a partner? The most likely candidate is the 10-crossing knot 10_6, whose own unknotting number is still unknown (it is 2 or 3).
Informal statement: Write $u(K)$ for the unknotting number and $\#$ for connected sum. Knots $K,K'$ are symbionts if $u(K\#K')<u(K)+u(K')$. * Polygonal knots: a list `l` of vertices in ℝ³ (closed polygon, edge from the last vertex back
  to the first), embedded (`Simple`: ≥ 3 vertices and the PL parametrization `param` is
  injective on [0, n)). Every tame knot has polygonal representatives, so knot types = classes
  of polygonal knots.
* Knot type (`Iso`): equivalence closure of three elementary moves: cyclic relabelling
  (`rotate 1`), subdivision of the first edge at an interior point, and a straight-line slide of
  the first vertex along which every intermediate polygon is embedded. Rotation lets these act
  anywhere. Reidemeister's Δ-move (replace edge [a,b] by [a,c] ∪ [c,b] when the triangle abc
  meets the knot only in [a,b]) is a subdivision followed by a slide of the new vertex, and its
  inverse is in the closure. Conversely every move is realised by a PL ambient isotopy. So
  `Iso` is exactly PL ambient isotopy of oriented polygonal knots (Reidemeister 1927), which is
  the same as ambient isotopy of tame knots. Mirror images are not identified (no reflection
  move), and orientation is kept (no reversal move).

* `trefoil`: 12 integer points sampled from the (2,3) torus knot and rounded. Checked
  numerically: the polygon is embedded (minimum distance between non-adjacent edges ≈ 12.8,
  much larger than the rounding error) and a generic projection has 5 crossings with knot
  determinant 3; the only knot of crossing number ≤ 5 with determinant 3 is the trefoil.
* Crossing change (`CrossChange`): the first vertex slides along a straight line and the
  intermediate polygons are embedded at all times except one time t₀ ∈ (0,1), at which the
  polygon has exactly one double point (exactly one parameter pair; triple points, tangential
  overlaps along segments or collapsed edges give more pairs, hence are excluded). Passing one
  strand through another once changes the knot by one crossing change (or, for a non-transverse
  touch, not at all); conversely every crossing change of a diagram is realised this way after
  an isotopy that makes a short edge pair pass through the other strand. So the minimal number
  of such moves is the unknotting number. `Unk m l` = l can be unknotted with m crossing
  changes, interleaved with isotopies; `unknottingNumber l = sInf {m | Unk m l}` (nonempty for
  every knot, so no junk). The unknot is a planar triangle.
* Connected sum (`IsSum P Q`): P lies in the half-space x₀ ≤ 0 meeting the plane x₀ = 0 exactly
  in its closing edge [a,b] (P = b, …, a), Q lies in x₀ ≥ 0 meeting the plane exactly in its
  closing edge [c,d] (Q = d, …, c), and a,b,c,d bound an embedded planar quadrilateral in
  x₀ = 0. That quadrilateral is a band disk meeting P ∪ Q only in [a,b] ∪ [c,d], and the
  concatenation `P ++ Q` (edges a→d and c→b replace [a,b], [c,d]) is the standard connected sum
  of the oriented knots P and Q (separated by a 2-sphere meeting it in two points). Since the
  trefoil is invertible, orientation conventions do not affect u(3₁ # K).

  trefoil; replacing both by mirrors preserves unknotting numbers, so this covers "some choice
  of mirror image". We state the symbiont inequality u(P # Q) < u(P) + u(Q) with P a trefoil
  (u(3₁) = 1, so this is u(3₁ # K) < 1 + u(K)).
* Proving `Claim` = the trefoil has a symbiont. Proving `¬Claim` = u(3₁ # K) = 1 + u(K) for
  every knot K.

noncomputable section

/-- Points of `ℝ³` (Euclidean). -/
abbrev E3 : Type := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)

/-- Vertex `k` of the closed polygon with vertex list `l` (indices taken mod the length). -/
def vtx (l : List E3) (k : ℕ) : E3 := l.getD (k % l.length) 0

/-- Piecewise-linear parametrization: on `[i, i+1]` it runs along the edge from vertex `i` to
vertex `i+1`; on `[0, n)` (n = number of vertices) it traverses the polygon once. -/
def param (l : List E3) (s : ℝ) : E3 :=
  (1 - (s - (⌊s⌋₊ : ℝ))) • vtx l ⌊s⌋₊ + (s - (⌊s⌋₊ : ℝ)) • vtx l (⌊s⌋₊ + 1)

/-- Double points of the polygon: parameter pairs `0 ≤ s < s' < n` with the same image. -/
def doublePts (l : List E3) : Set (ℝ × ℝ) :=
  {q : ℝ × ℝ | 0 ≤ q.1 ∧ q.1 < q.2 ∧ q.2 < (l.length : ℝ) ∧ param l q.1 = param l q.2}

/-- A polygonal knot: at least 3 vertices and the closed polygon is embedded (this also forces
consecutive vertices to be distinct). -/
def Simple (l : List E3) : Prop := 3 ≤ l.length ∧ doublePts l = ∅

/-- The polygon `x :: r` with its first vertex moved to `(1-t)x + t x'`. -/
def movePath (x x' : E3) (r : List E3) (t : ℝ) : List E3 := ((1 - t) • x + t • x') :: r

/-- Elementary isotopy moves: cyclic relabelling, subdivision of an edge, and a straight-line
slide of one vertex during which the polygon stays embedded. -/
inductive Move : List E3 → List E3 → Prop
  | rot (l : List E3) : Simple l → Move l (l.rotate 1)
  | sub (x y p : E3) (r : List E3) : Simple (x :: y :: r) → p ∈ openSegment ℝ x y →
      Move (x :: y :: r) (x :: p :: y :: r)
  | slide (x x' : E3) (r : List E3) :
      (∀ t ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, Simple (movePath x x' r t)) → Move (x :: r) (x' :: r)

/-- Same (oriented) knot type: the equivalence closure of `Move` (zig-zag chains). -/
inductive Iso : List E3 → List E3 → Prop
  | refl (l : List E3) : Iso l l
  | fwd {a b c : List E3} : Move a b → Iso b c → Iso a c
  | bwd {a b c : List E3} : Move b a → Iso b c → Iso a c

/-- A trefoil (of one chirality): 12 integer points on the (2,3) torus knot
`((2 + cos 3t) cos 2t, (2 + cos 3t) sin 2t, sin 3t)`, `t = 2πk/12`, scaled by 10 and rounded. -/
def trefoil : List E3 :=
  [!₂[(30 : ℝ), 0, 0], !₂[(10 : ℝ), 17, 10], !₂[(-5 : ℝ), 9, 0], !₂[(-20 : ℝ), 0, -10],
   !₂[(-15 : ℝ), -26, 0], !₂[(10 : ℝ), -17, 10], !₂[(10 : ℝ), 0, 0], !₂[(10 : ℝ), 17, -10],
   !₂[(-15 : ℝ), 26, 0], !₂[(-20 : ℝ), 0, 10], !₂[(-5 : ℝ), -9, 0], !₂[(10 : ℝ), -17, -10]]

/-- The unknot: a planar triangle. -/
def unknot : List E3 := [!₂[(0 : ℝ), 0, 0], !₂[(1 : ℝ), 0, 0], !₂[(0 : ℝ), 1, 0]]

/-- `l'` is obtained from `l` by one crossing change (one strand passed through another once). -/
def CrossChange (l l' : List E3) : Prop :=
  ∃ (x x' : E3) (r : List E3), l = x :: r ∧ l' = x' :: r ∧ Simple l ∧ Simple l' ∧
    ∃ t₀ ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1,
      (∀ t ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, t ≠ t₀ → Simple (movePath x x' r t)) ∧
      (doublePts (movePath x x' r t₀)).ncard = 1

/-- `l` can be unknotted by `m` crossing changes (with isotopies in between). -/
def Unk : ℕ → List E3 → Prop
  | 0, l => Iso l unknot
  | m + 1, l => ∃ l₁ l₂ : List E3, Iso l l₁ ∧ CrossChange l₁ l₂ ∧ Unk m l₂

/-- Unknotting number. -/
def unknottingNumber (l : List E3) : ℕ := sInf {m : ℕ | Unk m l}

/-- `P ++ Q` is the connected sum of the polygonal knots `P` and `Q` (see the notes). -/
def IsSum (P Q : List E3) : Prop :=
  ∃ (a b c d : E3) (mP mQ : List E3),
    P = b :: (mP ++ [a]) ∧ Q = d :: (mQ ++ [c]) ∧
    Simple P ∧ Simple Q ∧ Simple (P ++ Q) ∧
    a 0 = 0 ∧ b 0 = 0 ∧ c 0 = 0 ∧ d 0 = 0 ∧
    (∀ v ∈ mP, v 0 < 0) ∧ (∀ v ∈ mQ, 0 < v 0) ∧ Simple [a, b, c, d]

/-- The trefoil has a symbiont: some knot `K` with `u(3₁ # K) < u(3₁) + u(K)`. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ P Q : List E3, IsSum P Q ∧ Iso P trefoil ∧
    unknottingNumber (P ++ Q) < unknottingNumber P + unknottingNumber Q

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE047

  | slide (x x' : E3) (r : List E3) :
      (∀ t ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, Simple (movePath x x' r t)) → Move (x :: r) (x' :: r)

/-- Same (oriented) knot type: the equivalence closure of `Move` (zig-zag chains). -/
inductive Iso : List E3 → List E3 → Prop
  | refl (l : List E3) : Iso l l
  | fwd {a b c : List E3} : Move a b → Iso b c → Iso a c
  | bwd {a b c : List E3} : Move b a → Iso b c → Iso a c

/-- All edges of the closed polygon have the same length. -/
def Equilateral (l : List E3) : Prop :=
  ∀ k : ℕ, k < l.length → dist (vtx l k) (vtx l (k + 1)) = dist (vtx l 0) (vtx l 1)

/-- Stick number of the knot type of `l`. -/
def stick (l : List E3) : ℕ := sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ l' : List E3, Iso l l' ∧ l'.length = n}

/-- Equilateral stick number of the knot type of `l`. -/
def eqStick (l : List E3) : ℕ :=
  sInf {n : ℕ | ∃ l' : List E3, Iso l l' ∧ Equilateral l' ∧ l'.length = n}

def Claim : Prop := ∃ l : List E3, Simple l ∧ stick l < eqStick l

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE048

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E049: Ropelength lower bound for the trefoil
Tie a knot in a rope of thickness 1 using as little rope as possible. For the simplest knot, the trefoil, computer experiments find tight knots using about 16.37 units of rope. The last refereed proof shows that every knotted rope needs at least 15.66 units, and a 2026 computer-assisted preprint claims 15.76. Raise the proven lower bound for the trefoil substantially, ideally to 16.
Informal statement: For a $C^{1,1}$ simple closed curve $\gamma\subset\mathbb R^3$ let $\mathrm{Rop}(\gamma)=\mathrm{length}(\gamma)/(2\,\mathrm{reach}(\gamma))$ (length over tube diameter), and $R(3_1)=\inf\{\mathrm{Rop}(\gamma):\gamma\text{ a trefoil}\}$ (attained). Known: $15.66\le R(3_1)\lesssim16.372$ (refereed lower bound; numerical upper value), with an unrefereed claim $R(K)>15.7561$ for all nontrivial $K$. Formal target: a lower bound strictly beyond 15.7561, i.e. $R(3_1)>15.7561$, with a verifiable (here: Lean) proof; ideally $R(3_1)\ge16$.
Formalization notes:
* Curves: `γ : ℝ → ℝ³`, 1-periodic, C¹ with nowhere-vanishing derivative, injective on [0,1)
  (a regular embedded closed C¹ curve). Its image is `γ '' [0,1]`.
* Reach (Federer): sup of r ≥ 0 such that every point at distance < r from the image has a
  unique nearest point on it. For a closed C¹ curve, reach > 0 iff the curve is C^{1,1}, and the
  reach equals the thickness Δ[γ] (Gonzalez–Maddocks–Schuricht–von der Mosel); reach is finite
  for a closed curve, so the `sSup` is a real supremum. Curves of reach 0 have infinite
  ropelength and are excluded explicitly (avoiding the junk value x/0 = 0).
* Length = ∫₀¹ |γ'(t)| dt; Rop = length / (2·reach) (diameter convention, matching 15.66).
* Knot type: γ is a trefoil iff for all large N the inscribed polygon γ(0), γ(1/N), …,
  γ((N−1)/N) is a polygonal trefoil. For a regular embedded C¹ closed curve the inscribed
  polygons are, for N large, embedded and isotopic to γ, so this is the knot type of γ.
* Polygonal knots: a list `l` of vertices in ℝ³ (closed polygon, edge from the last vertex back
  to the first), embedded (`Simple`: ≥ 3 vertices and the PL parametrization `param` is
  injective on [0, n)). Every tame knot has polygonal representatives, so knot types = classes
  of polygonal knots.
* Knot type (`Iso`): equivalence closure of three elementary moves: cyclic relabelling
  (`rotate 1`), subdivision of the first edge at an interior point, and a straight-line slide of
  the first vertex along which every intermediate polygon is embedded. Rotation lets these act
  anywhere. Reidemeister's Δ-move (replace edge [a,b] by [a,c] ∪ [c,b] when the triangle abc
  meets the knot only in [a,b]) is a subdivision followed by a slide of the new vertex, and its
  inverse is in the closure. Conversely every move is realised by a PL ambient isotopy. So
  `Iso` is exactly PL ambient isotopy of oriented polygonal knots (Reidemeister 1927), which is
  the same as ambient isotopy of tame knots. Mirror images are not identified (no reflection
  move), and orientation is kept (no reversal move).

* `trefoil`: 12 integer points sampled from the (2,3) torus knot and rounded. Checked
  numerically: the polygon is embedded (minimum distance between non-adjacent edges ≈ 12.8,
  much larger than the rounding error) and a generic projection has 5 crossings with knot
  determinant 3; the only knot of crossing number ≤ 5 with determinant 3 is the trefoil.
* The infimum R(3₁) is attained, so "a bound beyond 15.7561" means exactly R(3₁) > 15.7561;
  `Claim` says: some L > 15.7561 bounds the ropelength of every trefoil from below. (This is the
  2026 preprint's claimed inequality specialised to the trefoil; a formal proof of it, or of
  anything stronger such as L = 16, is what is asked.) The best refereed bound is 15.66.
  Proving `Claim` = R(3₁) > 15.7561. Proving `¬Claim` = R(3₁) ≤ 15.7561 (refuting the preprint).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE049
noncomputable section

/-- Points of `ℝ³` (Euclidean). -/
abbrev E3 : Type := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)

/-- Vertex `k` of the closed polygon with vertex list `l` (indices taken mod the length). -/
def vtx (l : List E3) (k : ℕ) : E3 := l.getD (k % l.length) 0

/-- Piecewise-linear parametrization: on `[i, i+1]` it runs along the edge from vertex `i` to
vertex `i+1`; on `[0, n)` (n = number of vertices) it traverses the polygon once. -/
def param (l : List E3) (s : ℝ) : E3 :=
  (1 - (s - (⌊s⌋₊ : ℝ))) • vtx l ⌊s⌋₊ + (s - (⌊s⌋₊ : ℝ)) • vtx l (⌊s⌋₊ + 1)

/-- Double points of the polygon: parameter pairs `0 ≤ s < s' < n` with the same image. -/
def doublePts (l : List E3) : Set (ℝ × ℝ) :=
  {q : ℝ × ℝ | 0 ≤ q.1 ∧ q.1 < q.2 ∧ q.2 < (l.length : ℝ) ∧ param l q.1 = param l q.2}

/-- A polygonal knot: at least 3 vertices and the closed polygon is embedded (this also forces
consecutive vertices to be distinct). -/
def Simple (l : List E3) : Prop := 3 ≤ l.length ∧ doublePts l = ∅

/-- The polygon `x :: r` with its first vertex moved to `(1-t)x + t x'`. -/
def movePath (x x' : E3) (r : List E3) (t : ℝ) : List E3 := ((1 - t) • x + t • x') :: r

/-- Elementary isotopy moves: cyclic relabelling, subdivision of an edge, and a straight-line
slide of one vertex during which the polygon stays embedded. -/
inductive Move : List E3 → List E3 → Prop
  | rot (l : List E3) : Simple l → Move l (l.rotate 1)
  | sub (x y p : E3) (r : List E3) : Simple (x :: y :: r) → p ∈ openSegment ℝ x y →
      Move (x :: y :: r) (x :: p :: y :: r)
  | slide (x x' : E3) (r : List E3) :
      (∀ t ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, Simple (movePath x x' r t)) → Move (x :: r) (x' :: r)

/-- Same (oriented) knot type: the equivalence closure of `Move` (zig-zag chains). -/
inductive Iso : List E3 → List E3 → Prop
  | refl (l : List E3) : Iso l l
  | fwd {a b c : List E3} : Move a b → Iso b c → Iso a c
  | bwd {a b c : List E3} : Move b a → Iso b c → Iso a c

/-- A trefoil (of one chirality): 12 integer points on the (2,3) torus knot
`((2 + cos 3t) cos 2t, (2 + cos 3t) sin 2t, sin 3t)`, `t = 2πk/12`, scaled by 10 and rounded. -/
def trefoil : List E3 :=
  [!₂[(30 : ℝ), 0, 0], !₂[(10 : ℝ), 17, 10], !₂[(-5 : ℝ), 9, 0], !₂[(-20 : ℝ), 0, -10],
   !₂[(-15 : ℝ), -26, 0], !₂[(10 : ℝ), -17, 10], !₂[(10 : ℝ), 0, 0], !₂[(10 : ℝ), 17, -10],
   !₂[(-15 : ℝ), 26, 0], !₂[(-20 : ℝ), 0, 10], !₂[(-5 : ℝ), -9, 0], !₂[(10 : ℝ), -17, -10]]

/-- A regular embedded closed `C¹` curve with period 1. -/
def IsClosedCurve (γ : ℝ → E3) : Prop :=
  ContDiff ℝ 1 γ ∧ (∀ t : ℝ, γ (t + 1) = γ t) ∧ (∀ t : ℝ, deriv γ t ≠ 0) ∧
    Set.InjOn γ (Set.Ico (0 : ℝ) 1)

/-- Federer's reach of a set. -/
def reach (S : Set E3) : ℝ :=
  sSup {r : ℝ | 0 ≤ r ∧ ∀ x : E3, Metric.infDist x S < r →
    ∃! y : E3, y ∈ S ∧ dist x y = Metric.infDist x S}

/-- Length of a 1-periodic `C¹` curve. -/
def curveLength (γ : ℝ → E3) : ℝ := ∫ t in (0 : ℝ)..1, ‖deriv γ t‖

/-- The curve has the knot type of the trefoil. -/
def IsTrefoil (γ : ℝ → E3) : Prop :=
  ∃ N₀ : ℕ, ∀ N : ℕ, N₀ ≤ N → Iso (List.ofFn fun k : Fin N => γ ((k : ℝ) / (N : ℝ))) trefoil

/-- `R(3₁) > 15.7561`. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ L : ℝ, (157561 / 10000 : ℝ) < L ∧
    ∀ γ : ℝ → E3, IsClosedCurve γ → IsTrefoil γ → 0 < reach (γ '' Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1) →
      L ≤ curveLength γ / (2 * reach (γ '' Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1))

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE049

title: Does Antihydra halt?
credit: bbchallenge community (Antihydra found 2024; reformulation by mxdys et al.); Ligocki, 'BB(6) is Hard (Antihydra)'
premise_risks: The TM ⇔ arithmetic equivalence rests on bbchallenge wiki and its formal proofs, not a refereed paper. M is self-contained either way.
Collatz-like; likely far beyond current methods
plain: Start with 8 and repeatedly multiply by 3/2, rounding down. Keep score: +2 for every even number you see and −1 for every odd number. Does the score ever go negative? This is exactly the question of whether a specific 6-state Turing machine, called Antihydra, ever halts. Answering it is the first obstacle to determining the sixth Busy Beaver number.
math: Let $a_0=8$ and $a_{n+1}=\lfloor 3a_n/2\rfloor$. For $n\ge1$ let $E_n=\#\{i<n:a_i\text{ even}\}$ and $O_n=\#\{i<n:a_i\text{ odd}\}$. Does there exist $n$ with $O_n>2E_n$? Equivalently (bbchallenge), does the 6-state 2-symbol Turing machine 1RB1RA_0LC1LE_1LD1LC_1LA0LB_1LF1RE_---0RA halt from a blank tape? The conjecture is that it never halts.
review_note: Known: Simulated to $2^{38}$ rule steps without halting (bbchallenge wiki). Under a random-walk heuristic (steps +2/−1), the chance of ever reaching −1 from the current score is about $10^{-2.87\times10^{10}}$ (wiki). It is listed as an undecided 'probviously non-halting' cryptid on the BB(6) wiki page; the current BB(6) champion exceeds $10\uparrow\uparrow10\uparrow\uparrow10\uparrow\uparrow8$ (mxdys, June 2025). BB(5) is determined (arXiv:2509.12337). Related: Mahler's 3/2 problem; Dubickas on integer sequences from linear maps. More BB(6) cryptids, all unresolved: arXiv:2610.22603 (2026).

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E050: Does Antihydra halt?
Start with 8 and repeatedly replace a by ⌊3a/2⌋. Score +2 for each even term and −1 for each odd term. Does the running score ever go negative?
Informal statement: With a₀ = 8, a_{n+1} = ⌊3aₙ/2⌋, E_n = #{i < n : aᵢ even}, O_n = #{i < n : aᵢ odd}, is O_n ≤ 2E_n for every n? (Equivalently, the 6-state TM 1RB1RA_0LC1LE_1LD1LC_1LA0LB_1LF1RE_---0RA never halts, per the bbchallenge wiki.)
Formalization notes: `a` is the Hydra/Antihydra orbit with ℕ floor division. The score after n terms is 2·E n − O n; since it moves by +2 or −1, it goes negative iff it hits −1, iff O n > 2·E n for some n. `Claim` = "Antihydra never halts" (the conjectured answer). `¬Claim` = Antihydra halts. The TM equivalence itself is not formalized.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE050

/-- The Antihydra orbit: a₀ = 8, a_{n+1} = ⌊3aₙ/2⌋. -/
def a : ℕ → ℕ
  | 0 => 8
  | n + 1 => 3 * a n / 2

/-- Number of even terms among a₀, …, a_{n-1}. -/
def E (n : ℕ) : ℕ := ((Finset.range n).filter (fun i : ℕ => Even (a i))).card

/-- Number of odd terms among a₀, …, a_{n-1}. -/
def O (n : ℕ) : ℕ := ((Finset.range n).filter (fun i : ℕ => ¬ Even (a i))).card

/-- Antihydra never halts. -/
def Claim : Prop := ∀ n : ℕ, O n ≤ 2 * E n

end OpenProblems.QEDE050

title: Translational tiling of the plane with two tiles: decidable?
credit: Yang & Zhang, arXiv 2506.19295 (open problem stated); Abel et al., arXiv 2509.07906 (Table 3)
premise_risks: Fast-moving area (k went 5→4→3 in 2025, and the 3D monotile in 2026); a late-2026 preprint could settle k=2
Connected vs. possibly-disconnected tiles may differ; the main statement allows arbitrary finite tiles
plain: You are given two shapes made of grid squares, and you may only slide copies of them around, never rotate them. Can copies of the two shapes cover the whole infinite grid with no gaps or overlaps? With one shape there is an algorithm that always answers this. With three shapes, one of them in several pieces, it was proved in 2025 that no algorithm can exist. Two shapes is the open case.
math: Given finite $F_1,F_2\subset\mathbb Z^2$, decide whether there exist $A_1,A_2\subseteq\mathbb Z^2$ with $(F_1+A_1)\sqcup(F_2+A_2)=\mathbb Z^2$, i.e. every point of $\mathbb Z^2$ lies in exactly one translate $F_j+a$, $a\in A_j$. Is this problem decidable? (Variant: also require $F_1,F_2$ to be connected polyominoes.)
review_note: Known: k=1: decidable (Beauquier–Nivat 1991 for polyominoes; Bhattacharya 2020, periodic tiling conjecture in $\mathbb Z^2$, for arbitrary finite $F$). k=3: co-RE-complete with three polyominoes, one disconnected and two connected of constant size; two trominoes suffice for a periodic subset of 2D (Abel, Akitaya, Chung, Demaine et al., 'Undecidability of Tiling with a Tromino', arXiv:2509.07906, 2025; Table 3 lists 2D/2 pieces/translation as OPEN). k=4, possibly disconnected: Yang–Zhang, arXiv:2506.19295 (2025), who list the two-tile case as open. k=5 connected: Kim, arXiv:2508.10067. Two tiles in $\mathbb Z^2\times G_0$: undecidable (Greenfeld–Tao, arXiv:2108.07902). With rotations, two tiles: undecidable (arXiv:2506.11628). A single polycube in 3D, translations only: undecidable (arXiv:2610.12392, Oct 2026).

/-! QED-E051: Translational tiling of the plane with two tiles: decidable?
Given two finite sets of grid cells, can translated copies (no rotations) of them tile ℤ² exactly? Is there an algorithm deciding this?
Informal statement: Is the set of pairs (F₁, F₂) of finite subsets of ℤ² such that ℤ² = (F₁ + A₁) ⊔ (F₂ + A₂) for some A₁, A₂ ⊆ ℤ² decidable?
Formalization notes: Tiles are given as lists of cells in ℕ × ℕ (every finite subset of ℤ² can be translated into the first quadrant, and tileability is translation invariant, so this loses nothing). Duplicates in a list are harmless (`cells` is a set). `TwoTiles F₁ F₂` says every z ∈ ℤ² lies in exactly one placed copy, where a copy is a pair (tile index, translation vector) with the vector in the corresponding Aⱼ. That is a disjoint exact cover. An empty tile is allowed (the instance then degenerates to one-tile tiling, which is decidable, so it creates no loophole). `Claim` = the problem is decidable (computable in Mathlib's Partrec sense). `¬Claim` = undecidable. The connected-polyomino variant is not encoded.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE051

/-- The cells of a tile, as a subset of ℤ². -/
def cells (F : List (ℕ × ℕ)) : Set (ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {z | ∃ p ∈ F, z = ((p.1 : ℤ), (p.2 : ℤ))}

/-- Translates of `F₁` and `F₂` tile ℤ² exactly. -/
def TwoTiles (F₁ F₂ : List (ℕ × ℕ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ A₁ A₂ : Set (ℤ × ℤ), ∀ z : ℤ × ℤ, ∃! q : Bool × (ℤ × ℤ),
    (q.1 = false ∧ q.2 ∈ A₁ ∧ z - q.2 ∈ cells F₁) ∨
    (q.1 = true ∧ q.2 ∈ A₂ ∧ z - q.2 ∈ cells F₂)

/-- Two-tile translational tiling of the plane is decidable. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ComputablePred (fun F : List (ℕ × ℕ) × List (ℕ × ℕ) => TwoTiles F.1 F.2)

end OpenProblems.QEDE051

title: A shape with Heesch number 7
credit: Heesch (1968); Bašić (2021); posed as a target by Epoch AI FrontierMath open problems

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E052: A shape with Heesch number 7
Some shapes cannot tile the whole plane but can still be surrounded by a ring of copies of themselves, and that ring by another ring, and so on, up to some limit. The number of rings possible is the shape's Heesch number. The record is 6, found in 2021. Find a shape whose Heesch number is finite but at least 7.
Informal statement: For a closed topological disk $T\subset\mathbb R^2$ that does not tile the plane, the Heesch number $H(T)$ is the largest $k$ such that there is a patch of congruent copies of $T$ made of $T$ surrounded by $k$ successive coronas. Each corona is a ring of copies covering a neighbourhood of the previous patch's boundary, and each intermediate union must be a closed disk (no holes). Exhibit $T$ with $7\le H(T)<\infty$. (The polyform version — a polyomino, polyhex or polyiamond with $7\le H<\infty$ — is a special case: such a polyform is a closed disk $T$, so it would prove the formal `Claim`.)
Formalization notes:
* Plane: `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)`; congruent copies are images `g '' T` under isometries
  `g : E ≃ᵢ E` (reflections allowed, as in Kaplan's Heesch computations).
* Closed topological disk: a set homeomorphic (as a subspace) to the closed unit disk. Such a set
  is compact with nonempty interior, so interior-disjoint copies are genuinely non-overlapping.
* k successive coronas (hole-free convention): cumulative finite patches A 0 = {T} ⊆ A 1 ⊆ … ⊆
  A k of copies, with pairwise disjoint interiors (stated for copies with different images, so
  symmetries of T giving the same copy are harmless), such that every union U_i of the copies in
  A i is a closed topological disk, U_i ⊆ interior U_{i+1} (the corona covers a neighbourhood of
  the previous patch, in particular surrounds it), and every new copy in A (i+1) \ A i touches
  U_i (corona tiles are adjacent to the previous patch).
* `HasCoronas T k` is monotone (drop the outer coronas), so H(T) = sup {k : HasCoronas T k}.
  "7 ≤ H(T) < ∞" is then `HasCoronas T 7 ∧ ∃ k, ¬ HasCoronas T k`; no definition of tiling
  is needed (a tile of the plane admits coronas of every order, so H < ∞ implies T does not
  tile).
* Proving `Claim` = a closed disk with finite Heesch number ≥ 7 exists. Proving `¬Claim` = every
  closed disk with finite Heesch number has H ≤ 6.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE052
noncomputable section

/-- The Euclidean plane. -/
abbrev E : Type := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)

/-- `S` is a closed topological disk. -/
def IsClosedDisk (S : Set E) : Prop := Nonempty (Metric.closedBall (0 : E) 1 ≃ₜ S)

/-- Union of the copies `g '' T`, `g ∈ A`. -/
def patchUnion (T : Set E) (A : Set (E ≃ᵢ E)) : Set E := ⋃ g ∈ A, g '' T

/-- `T` can be surrounded by `k` successive hole-free coronas. -/
def HasCoronas (T : Set E) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ A : ℕ → Set (E ≃ᵢ E),
    A 0 = {IsometryEquiv.refl E} ∧
    (∀ i : ℕ, i ≤ k → (A i).Finite ∧ IsClosedDisk (patchUnion T (A i))) ∧
    (∀ g ∈ A k, ∀ h ∈ A k, g '' T ≠ h '' T →
      Disjoint (interior (g '' T)) (interior (h '' T))) ∧
    (∀ i : ℕ, i < k →
      A i ⊆ A (i + 1) ∧
      patchUnion T (A i) ⊆ interior (patchUnion T (A (i + 1))) ∧
      ∀ g ∈ A (i + 1) \ A i, (g '' T ∩ patchUnion T (A i)).Nonempty)

/-- A closed disk with finite Heesch number at least 7. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ T : Set E, IsClosedDisk T ∧ HasCoronas T 7 ∧ ∃ k : ℕ, ¬ HasCoronas T k

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE052

review_note: Known: Order 3 is impossible: Stewart & Wormstein, 'Polyominoes of order 3 do not exist', JCTA 61 (1992) 130–136. Maltby, 'Trisecting a rectangle', JCTA 66 (1994): no non-rectangular 3-piece congruent dissection; M. Reid noted on math-fun that the 5-, 7- and 9-piece dissection cases remain open. Odd tilings, as opposed to odd minimal tilings, exist: Reid, 'Many L-shaped polyominoes have odd rectangular packings', Ann. Comb. 18 (2014) 341–357. OEIS A126140 (maximum order for n cells): 'No example of a non-rectangular polyomino is known for which its order is odd.'

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E053: A polyomino of odd order
Is there a non-rectangular polyomino whose order (fewest congruent copies tiling some rectangle) is odd?
Informal statement: For a polyomino P that tiles a rectangle with congruent copies (rotations and reflections allowed), ord(P) is the least number of copies in such a tiling. Does some non-rectangular P have ord(P) odd?
Formalization notes: Cells are points of ℤ × ℤ (unit squares indexed by lower-left corner). A polyomino is a nonempty finite cell set connected under edge-adjacency (|dx| + |dy| = 1). A congruent copy is the image under one of the 8 symmetries of ℤ² (optional coordinate swap, then signs e₁, e₂ ∈ ℤˣ = {±1}) followed by a translation; `place g` is injective, so a single copy never overlaps itself. `TilesRectWith P k` says k copies exactly partition an a × b rectangle with a, b ≥ 1 (cover plus pairwise disjointness). k = 0 is impossible because the rectangle is nonempty, and the empty set is excluded by `IsPolyomino`. `IsRect P` says P is a translate of an a × b rectangle, a, b ≥ 1. `Claim` = such an odd-order polyomino exists. `¬Claim` = every non-rectangular rectifiable polyomino has even order (or tiles no rectangle).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE053

/-- The a × b rectangle [0,a) × [0,b) of cells. -/
def rect (a b : ℕ) : Set (ℤ × ℤ) := {z | 0 ≤ z.1 ∧ z.1 < a ∧ 0 ≤ z.2 ∧ z.2 < b}

/-- `P` is a translate of a nonempty rectangle. -/
def IsRect (P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ (a b : ℕ) (t : ℤ × ℤ), 0 < a ∧ 0 < b ∧ ∀ z : ℤ × ℤ, z ∈ P ↔ z - t ∈ rect a b

/-- Edge-adjacent cells. -/
def Adj (p q : ℤ × ℤ) : Prop := |p.1 - q.1| + |p.2 - q.2| = 1

/-- `P` is a polyomino: nonempty and edge-connected. -/
def IsPolyomino (P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  P.Nonempty ∧ ∀ p ∈ P, ∀ q ∈ P,
    Relation.ReflTransGen (fun x y : ℤ × ℤ => x ∈ P ∧ y ∈ P ∧ Adj x y) p q

/-- A symmetry of ℤ² (swap flag, two signs, translation) applied to a cell. -/
def place (g : Bool × ℤˣ × ℤˣ × (ℤ × ℤ)) (p : ℤ × ℤ) : ℤ × ℤ :=
  ((g.2.1 : ℤ) * (if g.1 then p.2 else p.1) + g.2.2.2.1,
   (g.2.2.1 : ℤ) * (if g.1 then p.1 else p.2) + g.2.2.2.2)

/-- `k` congruent copies of `P` exactly tile some nonempty rectangle. -/
def TilesRectWith (P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (a b : ℕ) (c : Fin k → Bool × ℤˣ × ℤˣ × (ℤ × ℤ)), 0 < a ∧ 0 < b ∧
    (∀ z : ℤ × ℤ, z ∈ rect a b ↔ ∃ i : Fin k, ∃ p ∈ P, place (c i) p = z) ∧
    (∀ (i j : Fin k) (p q : ℤ × ℤ), p ∈ P → q ∈ P →
      place (c i) p = place (c j) q → i = j)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ), IsPolyomino P ∧ ¬ IsRect P ∧
    ∃ k : ℕ, Odd k ∧ TilesRectWith P k ∧ ∀ k' : ℕ, k' < k → ¬ TilesRectWith P k'

end OpenProblems.QEDE053

title: Is Grundy's game eventually periodic?
credit: Berlekamp, Conway & Guy, Winning Ways; computations by A. Flammenkamp
premise_risks: Computed range: '239' and '235' are superscript-lost renderings (2^39 and 2^35 most likely); not verified from a clean source
Classic problem with no clear modern angle
plain: In Grundy's game, players take turns splitting a pile of coins into two smaller piles of different sizes, and whoever cannot move loses. The game's theory reduces to one number per pile size, its Grundy value. These values have been computed for piles of hundreds of billions of coins and show no repeating pattern yet, though Berlekamp, Conway and Guy conjectured that they eventually repeat. Do they?
math: Let $g(0)=g(1)=g(2)=0$ and for $n\ge3$ let $g(n)=\operatorname{mex}\{g(a)\oplus g(b): a+b=n,\ 1\le a<b\}$, where $\oplus$ is bitwise XOR. Is $g$ eventually periodic, i.e. are there $N,p\ge1$ with $g(n+p)=g(n)$ for all $n\ge N$? (Weaker open question: is $g$ bounded?)
review_note: Known: Berlekamp–Conway–Guy (Winning Ways) conjecture eventual periodicity; Wikipedia says it is unresolved. Flammenkamp's octal-games page, Table 2 entry for Grundy's game: values computed for all n up to '239', most likely $2^{39}$ with the superscript lost. The largest known value is 297, attained at n = 21544358589, and 1287 rare values are known, the largest at 48399022. Wikipedia's text reads 'first 235 values', most likely $2^{35}$. OEIS A002188. Golomb's periodicity for finite subtraction games does not apply.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E054: Is Grundy's game eventually periodic?
In Grundy's game a move splits a heap into two nonempty heaps of different sizes. Is the sequence of Grundy values of single heaps eventually periodic?
Informal statement: Let g(n) = mex{ g(a) ⊕ g(b) : a + b = n, 1 ≤ a < b } (so g(0) = g(1) = g(2) = 0). Are there N and p ≥ 1 with g(n + p) = g(n) for all n ≥ N?
Formalization notes: Instead of defining g by well-founded recursion, `IsGrundy g` states the mex recursion: no option value equals g n, and every smaller value is an option value. A function satisfying it exists and is unique (strong induction on n), so quantifying over all such g is neither vacuous nor ambiguous. ⊕ is `^^^` (bitwise xor on ℕ). For n ≤ 2 there are no options, which forces g n = 0. `Claim` = eventual periodicity (the Berlekamp–Conway–Guy conjecture). `¬Claim` = not eventually periodic.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE054

/-- `g` satisfies the Grundy-value recursion of Grundy's game. -/
def IsGrundy (g : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ n : ℕ,
    (∀ a b : ℕ, 1 ≤ a → a < b → a + b = n → g n ≠ (g a ^^^ g b)) ∧
    (∀ m : ℕ, m < g n → ∃ a b : ℕ, 1 ≤ a ∧ a < b ∧ a + b = n ∧ (g a ^^^ g b) = m)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ g : ℕ → ℕ, IsGrundy g →
    ∃ N p : ℕ, 0 < p ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, N ≤ n → g (n + p) = g n

end OpenProblems.QEDE054
